query: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary and ternary subsets provide 16 candidate alloys, nine of which are single-phase FCC after thermomechanical processing. Early reports associated increasing constituent count with greater strength, but that simple relationship is no longer generally accepted. Despite extensive experimental and theoretical investigation, the origins of differences in deformation and failure behavior remain unresolved; practical interpretation must also account for constituent cost and overall cost-performance balance. What testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs these mechanical-property differences and why? Define a controlled investigation, the observations predicted relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, the limits within which the hypothesis should apply, the prior evidence supporting it, and an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The mechanical-property differences among equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni and its quaternary/ternary subsets are primarily governed by variations in local lattice distortion—which arise from differences in atomic size misfit—and the consequent effects on dislocation behavior (including stacking fault energy and critical resolved shear stress). In other words, selective removal or addition of elements (for example, removing Mn or another constituent) subtly alters the local bonding and lattice parameters, which in turn changes the dislocation core structure and slip system activation, leading to variations in strength–ductility trade-offs and failure behavior.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni processed by identical thermomechanical treatments to yield a single-phase FCC structure (the quinary baseline), along with analogous quaternary and ternary alloy subsets.
generation.intervention: Prepare alloy subsets by selectively removing (or varying the content of) a constituent element while maintaining similar thermomechanical processing routes to establish single-phase FCC structures, and then subject them to mechanical testing.
generation.conditions: All alloys are processed under identical thermomechanical routines to obtain single-phase FCC microstructures, tested at room temperature under quasi-static loading (e.g., nanoindentation and micropillar compression) to measure yield strength, critical resolved shear stress, and ductility.
generation.structural_mediator: Local lattice distortions and changes in stacking fault separation (reflecting modified dislocation core structures) induced by atomic size misfit variations.
generation.mechanism: Differences in constituent count modify the degree of local lattice distortion. Increased distortions raise solid solution strengthening by enhancing the CRSS and altering stacking fault energies, whereas reduced distortion (from a lower constituent count) lowers these barriers. This trade-off affects dislocation mobility and slip system activation, thereby governing the balance between strength and ductility.
generation.predicted_outcome: Relative to the equiatomic quinary baseline, alloy subsets with reduced constituent count (and hence lower lattice distortions) will exhibit a lower critical resolved shear stress and hardness, potentially trading some strength for improved ductility. Conversely, subsets that maintain or enhance atomic size mismatch may show increased strength but reduced uniform plastic deformation capabilities.
generation.baseline: The equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy processed to a single-phase FCC microstructure.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys fabricated by comparable thermomechanical processing at room temperature under quasi-static deformation; the effects may be different at extreme temperatures, in multiphase microstructures, or under dynamic loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: While the role of lattice distortion and stacking fault energy in strengthening is supported by trends in HEAs, the exact quantitative contributions to ductility and failure behavior, as well as the interplay with cost-performance factors, remain to be rigorously determined.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate the equiatomic Cr-Mn-Fe-Co-Ni high-entropy alloy (quinary baseline) as well as its selected quaternary and ternary subsets, ensuring each is processed into a single-phase FCC microstructure using identical thermomechanical treatments. Perform controlled mechanical tests (e.g., micropillar compression and nanoindentation) to measure critical resolved shear stress (CRSS), yield strength, and ductility. Additionally, use techniques such as transmission electron microscopy (TEM) to quantify dislocation structures and stacking fault separations.
measurements: Critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) from micropillar compression tests
Yield strength and hardness from nanoindentation
Stacking fault energy and local lattice distortions via high-resolution TEM and diffraction analysis
Tensile ductility assessed via uniaxial tensile tests
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the mechanical properties (i.e., strength, CRSS, and ductility) of the alloy subsets do not correlate in a consistent manner with the predicted changes in lattice distortion and stacking fault energy—as estimated from atomic size mismatch (for example, if subsets with reduced theoretical distortion show similar or higher CRSS and lower ductility compared to the quinary baseline)—then the hypothesis that local lattice distortion governs the observed differences in deformation and failure behavior would be refuted.

Size effect, critical resolved shear stress, stacking fault energy, and solid solution strengthening in the CrMnFeCoNi high-entropy alloy

Abstract: AbstractHigh-entropy alloys (HEAs) comprise a novel class of scientifically and technologically interesting materials. Among these, equatomic CrMnFeCoNi with the face-centered cubic (FCC) structure is noteworthy because its ductility and strength increase with decreasing temperature while maintaining outstanding fracture toughness at cryogenic temperatures. Here we report for the first time by single-crystal micropillar compression that its bulk room temperature critical resolved shear stress (CRSS) is ~33–43 MPa, ~10 times higher than that of pure nickel. CRSS depends on pillar size with an inverse power-law scaling exponent of –0.63 independent of orientation. Planar ½ < 110 > {111} dislocations dissociate into Shockley partials whose separations range from ~3.5–4.5 nm near the screw orientation to ~5–8 nm near the edge, yielding a stacking fault energy of 30 ± 5 mJ/m2. Processing and Properties of High-Entropy Ultra-High Temperature Carbides

Abstract: Bulk equiatomic (Hf-Ta-Zr-Ti)C and (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C high entropy Ultra-High Temperature Ceramic (UHTC) carbide compositions were fabricated by ball milling and Spark Plasma Sintering (SPS). It was found that the lattice parameter mismatch of the component monocarbides is a key factor for predicting single phase solid solution formation. The processing route was further optimised for the (Hf-Ta-Zr-Nb)C composition to produce a high purity, single phase, homogeneous, bulk high entropy material (99% density); revealing a vast new compositional space for the exploration of new UHTCs. One sample was observed to chemically decompose; indicating the presence of a miscibility gap. While this suggests the system is not thermodynamically stable to room temperature, it does reveal further potential for the development of new in situ formed UHTC nanocomposites.
